## Design

### 2026-10-17 – Day 1: Brainstorming

**6h**

Day 1: Brainstorming

Today, I started brainstorming ideas for my project. I quickly decided on a robotic arm. I have been in robotics for 6 years by now and have always wanted to make something along those lines. Furthermore, my friends and I have tried making robot dogs in the past, so this seemed like a good idea.

To start, I needed to learn how to use Onshape. This is my first time CADding, so I tried to learn the ropes. I watched a few tutorials for Onshape usage before settling on the Onshape course they offer. This course (for free, btw) was extremely useful and taught me most everything I needed for this project. I made a few sample projects to test my skills, so I spent a few hours on that matter.

Next, I started on my robot arm. First, I wanted to see if I could find a decent model to base my design on, and I found this.

![Screenshot 2026-10-17 133758](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/addcb483d7607c374b89c16e464f5a6e53b78130a2b1facb269c139290faf229.png)

This was going to be my model. A few changes I would make to it, reducing the freaking cost. This one robotic arm was costing $140, while my budget is $65. Next, I noticed that the entire thing looked to be metal, so I am changing that because I do not have the budget to spend on CNCing parts, and instead will 3d print everything from something like PCBWay. Furthermore, this robot is 5-axis, while I want it to be a 4-axis to reduce the number of motors.

Then I started my CAD. I started with the bottom layer:

![Screenshot 2026-10-17 132456](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/74bd3e9ed9c952e0a5a0e56118b7c8ceea1a65c2d0f341f3597d48b2d484817c.png)

This layer has space to house both the robot arm and the electronics (hopefully large enough). I also decided to create all of the layers that I made to be .25 cm tall.

Next, I made the next few layers, as well as separating everything with standoffs. Then I had to start searching for motors. I settled on the basic MG90S, which means Metal Gear 90 Servo. This motor will not allow my arm to turn 180 degrees, but it makes coding easy, so I am ok with it.

![Screenshot 2026-10-17 132549](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/e738a9b72f2ec4560322b494a536b4ce6a7766a93537ca7f248ce147b5130ddf.png)

Then I made the layer that the servo connects to for stability. This part was decently easy, with the measure tool coming in clutch in Onshape. Then I started working on the turntable. Basically, at the bottom of the arm, there must be a turntable-like mechanism to help everything turn smoothly, so I sandwiched the turntable between the top two layers of the base.

![Screenshot 2026-10-17 132504](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/db4c79f5901cb1ba81a4e187111072ed2633814619aa83c26160b3b697acfe8c.png)

Connecting the turntable to the servo was difficult. I could not figure out how to create a gear in Onshape because the plan was to make a gear-sized indent in the perfect shape of the servo's metal gear. That way, they would just slot together, and it would be easy.

I first tried to make even trapezoids along the length of the circle. Not only was this time-consuming, but it also never came out perfectly even (this was before I knew about circular patterns). Then I switched to making 2 circles and creating triangles between the two that would cut out the shape of the gear. This was decently promising.

![Screenshot 2026-10-16 225848](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/7f227175684b953d2a5a0bed0797b94a6abb8be971709a38c15cdab04043c6fc.png)

However, when I took it into an assembly to check, I realized that this would not mesh together well. The reason was discovered in the way they make the gear. the gears sides are chamfered, so when taking measurements, you have to do some pythagorean theorem. I would do this, but the gear is not sharp at the edges; it is rounded. This means I cannot take an accurate measurement for this calculation.

![Screenshot 2026-10-17 132444](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/1e7d44a2899f595ebd6d7cf36016fc26e383b7496599b10e05da6c7484f9b3c0.png)

However, it was getting pretty late, so I put everything into 1 assembly and called it a day.

![Screenshot 2026-10-17 132523](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/ba1eb0ed6655a08f0e3dfda78e513bd24f20b95e548d74d1a9b13476a2d79414.png)

Things I need to do next time: fix the meshing (probably use the servo attachment) and create most of the rest of the arm

### 2026-10-17 – Even though my recording was 1 hr, I actually worked for 3 because I forgot to hit record again after eating lunch. During this time, I was mainly working on the servo's connection to the turntable. I

**3.23h**

Even though my recording was 1 hr, I actually worked for 3 because I forgot to hit record again after eating lunch. During this time, I was mainly working on the servo's connection to the turntable. I was modifying the model of the servo arm a lot during the time that it was not recording. The holes on the servo connector and the turntable were not matching up, which was visible in the timelapse, but it did not show how long it took me to fix that design.

I have a few photos of my failed attempts, but not many. First, I tried to research the correct sizes again, also looking at the servo arm that I have on my person. I measured that and tried to emulate it in the design to see if it was a system error or if they made the servo that I imported incorrectly, but that did not really work for a few reasons.

![WIN_20261017_17_29_03_Pro](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/ebb8f3a934d3a2fa7a622ed29fe14701ba9c6d1288b529b4b27f12a8e715790e.jpg)

![WIN_20261017_17_30_05_Pro](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/6e0660b430668f43596461c843d724d6eea0c4b0e2c875bb76122c0f70488219.jpg)

These show that I was measuring an SG90S, not the MG90S. While the sizing differences seem dismissible between the two, it was a huge problem because of how small the units and holes were.

Then I switched over to using the measure tool in Onshape. The measure tool was showing me that the system was off by a certain x and y value. I inputted this into the connector, but the holes on the other side were then off by another value. After like an hour, I realized that it was a rotation error and I fixed that issue, but the holes were still off by a bit, and that is around (give or take) where the video picks up again. Thanks for understanding, and I hope it is ok that it wasn't recorded!

### 2026-10-18 – Final Entry: Parts

**5.5h**

Final Entry: Parts

Today was all spent looking at prices.

First, I worked on finding deals for my 3d printed mechanism. I knew it would be expensive because, in total, I had 12 parts being printed, and the robotic arm is definitely not small, so the expected price was already $30 in my mind. $30 is a lot, but also decently manageable.

I first looked at CraftCloud. Gemini told me that CraftCloud has the best quality for price. They are a company that is based overseas in Germany. CraftCloud was working decently well for me, and I got a good quote too at just $25. It was a decent quote, so I went through with it and went to checkout. There I noticed a $30 shipping fee. With just my 3d print, my budget was over. In hindsight, it kind of makes sense because they are based in Germany.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/c253c548c7e6e22e1525e8bfddc8cdfc6bae2f545a49f6ce3f9041c392124cf7.png)

Next, I went on to look at PCBWay. I have heard a lot of great things about PCBWay from many different engineering YouTube channels. They, too, charged way too much, but from a different perspective. For them, shipping was minimal at only $5, but each part was ~$5, so that added up quickly given the amount of parts that I had.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/5624f33bc2a232bb4f96332084819e06a230a91670c4e875a1b3328f8c29e6ff.png)

Finally, I turned to JLC3DP. This brand was actually reasonable, with prices being extremely low, and they only charged $8 for shipping, though you have to keep in mind it takes longer to ship. This brand took me a while to find because originally, I thought the JLC brand was specific to PCB Design, because it was the manufacturer I used in PCB last week. However, after a lot of digging, I managed to find this.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/706da94ae85f546a8e6779820903139a707729c79942a8976912fa792c1e0716.png)

A mini struggle I had when looking at JLCPCB was finding the low shipping cost. Originally, shipping was a grand total of $20. While this looked OK on paper, it was not feasible because I needed to buy other things and keep in mind taxes. After quite a bit of digging, I managed to discover the General Shipping routes and USPS, which both had really low shipping prices, so I selected those and moved on.

While working, I noticed that my total for my parts was still very high at $35 before taxes, so I tried to see how to shrink it. I was looking for screws and joystick modules, so I knew I would not be able to have all of the parts I wanted. It was also getting very late, so I knew I couldn't change my CAD to make the functionality work with modification. After a lot of deliberation, I came to the difficult decision to do away with the claw at the end of the robot.

This decision was a very difficult one for me. Removing the entire claw took away all of the functionality of the build. However, it was the only sacrifice I could make. You see, the build went straight from base to claw, and no part of it could be taken out without removing support for the part above it, except for, well, the top of the build, which was the claw. I also thought that it would still be a fun build to make, because it is still an arm, just not one with a hand.

Next, I began my search for my servo motors. I knew that the servos had to be the MG90S, because that is what I based my entire build on. You see, the MG90S motors are great because they are small like the SG90S, but they are made of metal, essentially doubling the torque and efficiency. They were relatively easy to find, as almost all stalls and stores had them, but the pricing was a huge issue. Since the MG90S was made of metal, many companies jacked up the price under the pretense that metal just costs that much more. I also needed mine in a pack of 4 or more for a good price, and that was very difficult to find. If I searched on AliExpress or Alibaba, I found sellers with great prices, but those great prices were soft-locked behind 1st time buyers. Next, Amazon also had a huge collection, which took me a while to look through, but their prices were egregiously high, so much so that they would not fit in my budget. Then I started combing through random online dealers, but all of them had low prices and insane shipping costs. Finally, I randomly stumbled upon Walmart of all places selling a pack of 4 for a reasonable price, so I am pretty happy about that deal.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/289755e87fe32830d36b1f64576a62208c9e2825a9bb00982877b2a0f9cb659e.png)

Next, I started to look for my screws. For my build, I used a variety of M2 and M3 screws, so I needed both, along with nuts to fasten them. I started my search on Amazon, trying to find them separately, but I ran into the same problem I had earlier, which was that they cost way too much. Then I looked through places like Home Depot and Walmart, hoping to find a good deal, but they also cost like $10 for 1 case. Finally,  I settled upon a cheap AliExpress M2 kit with nuts and an M3 kit with nuts, together totaling around $12.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/d8c61101b6d9bf9ab54ddbc524ad8fd4e7d566fb124be12ebe3e80b47c1b79eb.png)

Finally, I looked for a joystick module. I decided to use joystick modules because they are intuitive and easy to control, unlike small buttons. I already had 1 at home, so I really only needed  1 more, because the plane was to map 1 axis to 1 motor. I again started on Amazon, went to Home Depot and Walmart, before ending at AliExpress and buying the final part of my project.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/dea2d8abf360c7e69d469d6e141b8fa30a7a1f34b6b97acedc2e5b6e868e91da.png)

Thanks to Hack Club again for sponsoring me. This week's project is named: The Thing (I think it's funny because the thing is just a hand with no arm, and my project is an arm with no hand)
